title: Normal and Not

post.author: u/parish_register_wynfrith
post.title: I volunteer nights at a family history society. On Monday a member proved her great-great-aunt died in 1891. Tonight that aunt is still sitting in a photograph from 1900, in 37 of our family trees.

blocks.text: I'm a night volunteer at the Thornleigh Family History Society. After work I transcribe old parish registers into our database, usually until two. The database has a person table: every person once, with their birth, death and parents. Members build family trees from those people. We have 412 trees now, and the biggest run to about 400 people.

In 2014 a volunteer called Alcuin Treharne found the big trees took nearly two seconds to draw. So he added a tree table. When someone is added to a tree, their name, dates and parents are copied into a row for that tree, and a tree page reads only its own rows. The tree table holds 41,236 rows, and the pages open in a blink. Each tree page also hangs the society's old photographs on their years, and names everyone in the tree who was alive that year.

On Monday at 10:14, Sabine Hosken, one of our members, corrected her great-great-aunt, Lavinia Gorrandine. Our records said Lavinia died in 1919. Sabine had found her burial in a register I transcribed in the spring: 14 March 1891. She changed the death date on Lavinia's person page and pressed Save.

Mon 10:14:00.000  person P-20417  Lavinia Gorrandine  death 1919 -> 1891
                  UPDATE person  1 row  40 ms  saved
Mon 10:14:00.040  person page P-20417   1852 to 1891
Thu 23:12:06      tree T-0288 (Hosken)  Lavinia Gorrandine  1852 to 1919
                  photo 1900, census year: 8 people, 9 names
Thu 23:14:51      trees with P-20417: 37 of 412   showing 1919: 37

Her person page says 1852 to 1891. Tonight I opened Sabine's tree to check the burial link, and there was Lavinia, 1852 to 1919. The 1900 photograph hung beside her: the household on a bench outside the farmhouse. Eight people on the bench. Nine names in the caption, and hers is last, *seated, right*. At the right end of the bench there is only a dark shape I keep telling myself is a coat.
She had been in the churchyard for nine years by then.

I checked every tree she's in. She is in 37 of our 412, and all 37 say 1919. Nobody has touched them since Monday. Kesia, who looks after our database, says nothing in the tree table knows the person table changed. The committee wants a rule by Saturday: whoever fixes a person fixes every tree she's in, by hand. Kesia would rather fix the database. What should she do?

blocks.label: lavinia_rows_thursday.png

diagram.aria: Kesia's drawing on Thursday at 23:14. Sabine's save on Monday at 10:14 changed Lavinia's death date from 1919 to 1891 in the person table, the source of truth, and the person page shows 1852 to 1891. The tree table, 412 trees and 41,236 rows, got Lavinia's row copied once, when she was added to each tree, and has had no refresh since: her 37 rows say 1919. The tree pages read the tree table, so all 37 of her trees are wrong, and the 1900 photograph shows 8 people and 9 names.

blocks.caption: Kesia's drawing on Thursday night. Sabine's save changed one row: Lavinia's person row, which the person page reads. Her name and dates were copied into the tree table once, when she was added to each of her 37 trees, and nothing has refreshed them since. Tree pages read only the tree table, so all 37 still say 1919, and the 1900 photograph names nine people on a bench of eight.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Count before you fix. Tonight, in how many places is Lavinia's death date written? Which of them does the society treat as the truth, and which were made from it? When Sabine pressed Save at 10:14, how many of those places changed, and what was supposed to change the rest? Then ask the other question: why does the tree table exist at all? Alcuin had a reason in 2014. Time the 400-person tree drawn straight from the person table, against the same tree read from its own rows. Whatever you choose has to answer two things: what a tree page costs on every view, and how long any tree may say 1919 after a fix. Write both numbers down before you pick.

replies.author: u/parish_register_wynfrith
replies.text: Kesia timed it on her test copy. The 400-person tree takes 1,640 ms from the person table and 60 ms from its tree rows. Alcuin wasn't wrong about the speed.

comments.author: u/joins_cost_nothing_ivo
comments.text: Normalize everything, joins are free. To normalize is to store each fact once, in the table it's about, and point at it by its key everywhere else. Codd's 1970 paper was already worried about redundancy and consistency. A fact stored twice will disagree with itself one day, and your tree table stores every fact once per tree. Drop it and build each tree page from the person table with a join. Joining is what databases are for. If a 400-person tree takes 1.6 seconds, find the missing index; that's not a reason to keep copies.

comments.author: u/rebuild_at_two_quenby
comments.text: Our society had the same kind of table, and we stopped trying to keep it fresh during the day. Every night at 02:00 a script rebuilds the whole tree table from the person table, and it's done by about 02:40. Nothing extra happens when anyone presses Save, so nothing in the save can break, and every correction is in every tree by breakfast. Most of our members only look at their trees in the evening anyway.

replies.author: u/parish_register_wynfrith
replies.text: Kesia says ours would rewrite all 41,236 rows a night. She likes how simple it is. The committee still likes its rule: about 2 minutes a tree, by hand.

reply.prompt: Kesia can change the database before Saturday's committee meeting. What should she do about the tree table? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Drop the tree table and build each tree page from the person table on every view, with a join. Each fact is stored once, so nothing can disagree.
options.verdict: Correct, and slow on every view
options.part2: Kesia dropped the tree table on Friday night. Every tree page now builds from the person table, and every page is right the moment a person changes: Lavinia left the 1900 photograph at once. But the 400-person trees take 1,640 ms to draw instead of 60, and every view pays it again, 4 ms a person, for every member who opens one. The small trees hardly notice: a 12-person tree takes 88 ms. At Saturday's meeting the treasurer opened the Gorrandine tree on the projector, and the committee watched it draw. Kesia is now building the tree table again, the way Alcuin did in 2014. This time she is writing down who refreshes it.
options.senior: Normalizing removes the update anomaly by removing the copies, and it's the right starting point. But the reads pay for it on every view, and here reads outnumber corrections by far: a 400-person tree costs 1,640 ms built from the person table against 60 ms from its own rows. An index helps each lookup, not the 400 of them. Keep the copy that makes the common read cheap, and make it safe: one owner of the truth, copies derived from it, and a refresh rule.

options.text: Keep the tree table and adopt the committee's rule: whoever fixes a person opens every tree she appears in and fixes her row there by hand.
options.part2: The rule started on Saturday. Kesia printed the list of Lavinia's 37 trees and I fixed them on Sunday evening, 2 minutes a tree: 74 minutes, one after another, so the last tree said 1919 for 74 minutes after I began. Every fix is its own save: 38 rows and 3,000 ms of database time for one correction, against 40 for the save alone. On Wednesday another volunteer corrected a man who is in 52 trees, fixed 9 of them before midnight and meant to finish the next day. Nothing in the database knows which 43 are left. A member found one of them on Friday.
options.senior: A rule that lives in people's heads is a refresh rule with no owner and no check. It's slow (2 minutes a tree), it scales with how many trees a person is in, and it fails silently: a tree nobody remembers stays wrong until somebody stumbles on it. Copies need a refresh the database does every time, from the one owner of the truth, plus a check that finds any copy that drifted.

options.text: Keep the tree table, and rebuild all of it from the person table every night at 02:00, so any fix reaches every tree by the next morning.
options.verdict: Trade-off: right by morning, wrong all day
options.part2: Kesia set up the rebuild on Friday. It reads the person table at 02:00 and swaps the new tree table in at 02:40, rewriting all 41,236 rows every night, and on Saturday morning Lavinia's 37 trees said 1891. Then the windows began to show. The next Monday a member corrected a birth date at 10:14, and her trees kept the old one until 02:40 on Tuesday: 16 h 26 min. On Wednesday a correction saved at 02:10, after that night's reading, waited a whole extra night: 1 d 0 h 30 min. I save most of my transcriptions between midnight and two, so most of mine now wait a day.
options.senior: A scheduled rebuild is simple, adds nothing to the save, and repairs every drift each night, which is why so many teams start there. Its price is the window: every correction is wrong in every copy until the next rebuild finishes, from minutes to more than a day, and the job rewrites everything to change a few rows. PostgreSQL's REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW works the same way. Use it when the copies may be a day old, and say so.

options.text: Keep the person table as the only truth; refresh her tree rows from it in the same transaction or a queue, and check nightly that both agree.
options.part2: Kesia added an index on the tree table's person column and changed Save into one transaction: BEGIN, update the person row, update every tree row for that person, COMMIT. For Lavinia that's 4 round trips, 160 ms, 38 rows, and the person page and her 37 trees can't disagree, even for a moment. Tree pages still read their own rows: 60 ms for the 400-person trees. She added a check at 03:00 that compares every tree row with the person table. On its first night it found Lavinia's 37 rows still saying 1919, from Monday, repaired them and sent her an alert. It has found nothing since. For anyone in hundreds of trees she has a change queue ready: the save stays at 160 ms, a worker updates the trees about a minute later, 240 ms of database time in all. On Saturday night I opened Sabine's tree again. Eight people on the bench. Eight names.
options.senior: Denormalize on purpose: one owner of the truth, copies derived from it and never edited on their own, a refresh rule written down, and a check that proves the copies agree. Refreshing in the same transaction makes the copy as correct as the truth, at the cost of a bigger write; a change queue keeps the write small and accepts a stated delay. The nightly check catches what both miss, such as a script that writes around the save.

sim.title: Model the trees at the Thornleigh Family History Society
sim.lede: You're Kesia, replaying Lavinia's correction. The society has 412 trees and a tree table of 41,236 rows; Lavinia is in 37 trees, so she has one person row and 37 tree rows. The clock opens two minutes before Sabine's save and runs 10 seconds a second. Pick a storage model: tree copies with no refresh (as now); fixed by hand, 2 minutes a tree; normalized only, with no tree table, so every page is built from the person table with joins; refreshed in the same transaction as the save; refreshed from a change queue, where a worker applies the change after the delay you pick; or rebuilt nightly, where a job reads the person table at 02:00 and swaps the new table in at 02:40. The cost model: every statement is one round trip to the database, 40 ms. A tree page that reads its own rows costs 40 ms plus 0.05 ms a person; one built from the person table costs 40 ms plus 4 ms a person, walking the parent links and joining each person's facts. A tree is wrong while the person row says 1891 and its copy still says 1919. The nightly check at 03:00 compares every tree row with the person table and repairs any that differ. The stats show her trees showing 1919, the longest a tree showed 1919 (measured from the moment Sabine pressed Save, rounded to the second), tree page time, database time and rows touched per correction, and tree rows rewritten each night. Changing anything but the tree size replays from the start. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Skip 1 minute three times. As now, the save changes one row and all 37 of her trees say 1919. Skip to Thursday 23:12 and read the log: 3 d 12:58:00, and a photograph with 9 names. Turn the nightly check on and skip to Tuesday 03:30: it finds the 37 at 03:00, 16:46:00 after the save. Pick normalized only: nothing is ever wrong, but a 400-person page takes 1,640 ms; try 12 people. Pick the same transaction: 160 ms, 38 rows, never wrong, pages at 60 ms. Try the change queue at 60 s and at 5 minutes, and see how long the trees stay wrong. Pick the nightly rebuild: 16:26:00 for a 10:14 save; then move the save to 02:10 and watch a correction miss a night. Last, fix by hand: 1:14:00 if a volunteer starts at once, and 3,000 ms of database time.

explain.oneLine: Lavinia's death date lived in 38 places, and the save changed one. The tree table was a copy kept for speed with nothing to refresh it, so 37 trees kept her alive and the photograph kept her seat.

steps.title: One fact, 38 places.
steps.text: Lavinia's death date was written in 38 places: her row in the person table, and her row in each of the 37 trees she appears in. Sabine's save changed one of them. Nothing told the other 37, so they still say 1919, and a tree page draws only from its own rows. The photograph's caption names everyone the tree says was alive in 1900, so it names her. That's an update anomaly: a fact copied into many places goes out of step when one copy changes. William Kent's 1983 guide to normal forms gives the textbook version: "If the address of the warehouse changes, every record referring to a part stored in that warehouse must be updated." And: "Because of the redundancy, the data might become inconsistent, with different records showing different addresses". Nobody at Thornleigh made a mistake on Monday. The design made one changed row look like a finished correction.

steps.title: Normalization: each fact once, in its own place.
steps.text: Normalization means storing each fact once, in the table it's about, and pointing at it by its key from everywhere else. E. F. Codd's 1970 paper, which introduced the relational model, proposed "a normal form for data base relations". Kent's guide gives a line for each of the first three normal forms, and they fit in plain words. First normal form: every field holds one value, with no lists or repeating groups inside a row (Kent: "all occurrences of a record type must contain the same number of fields"). Second normal form: no field is about only part of the key. "Second normal form is violated when a non-key field is a fact about a subset of a key." Alcuin's tree table has a composite key, tree and person together, and Lavinia's name and dates are about the person alone, so they repeat once per tree: that's the break. Third normal form: no field is about another non-key field, such as a parent's name stored beside the parent's id. Kent's summary: a non-key field is a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

steps.title: Why Alcuin copied anyway.
steps.text: Normalized data costs reads. Kent says the normalization rules "tend to penalize retrieval", and that "there is no obligation to fully normalize all records when actual performance requirements are taken into account." Kesia's timing shows why Alcuin built his table: the 400-person tree takes 1,640 ms from the person table, walking the parent links and joining each person's facts, and 60 ms from its own tree rows, on every view. Keeping a copy for reads is denormalization, and it's an ordinary engineering choice. It is usually safe when three things hold: one owner of the truth (the person table), copies derived from it and never edited on their own, and a written rule for refreshing them. Alcuin's table had the first two and not the third. It's the cache from the bakery and the dairy cases again, with no invalidation. Databases offer a built-in version: PostgreSQL's materialized view stores a query's result like a table, and its docs say reading it "is often much faster than accessing the underlying tables directly or through a view", but "the data is not always current".

steps.title: Refresh rules, and a check.
steps.text: There are three common refresh rules, and the sim prices each. In the same transaction: the save becomes BEGIN, update the person row, update every tree row for that person, COMMIT. Both change together or neither does: 4 round trips, 160 ms, 38 rows, and no tree is ever wrong. It needs an index on the tree table's person column, or that update reads all 41,236 rows to find 37. From a change queue: the save writes the person row and a change row in one transaction, and a worker applies the change to the tree rows afterwards. The save stays short however many trees a person is in, and the trees are wrong only for the queue's delay, a minute in the sim. On a schedule: simple, with nothing extra in the save, but a 10:14 correction shows at 02:40 the next day, 16 h 26 min later, and one made at 02:10, after that night's reading, waits 1 d 0 h 30 min. Fixing by hand works only while every volunteer remembers every tree. Whatever the rule, add a check: at 03:00, compare every tree row with the person table, repair any difference and raise an alert. As now, it would have found Lavinia's 37 rows on the first night.

steps.title: Start from the questions.
steps.text: Designing for access patterns means listing the queries first and shaping the data to answer them. AWS's DynamoDB guidance puts it plainly: "you shouldn't start designing your schema for DynamoDB until you know the questions it will need to answer." Thornleigh's questions are: show one person, show one tree, list the trees a person is in, and correct a person. Corrections are rare and tree views constant, which is why a derived tree table pays, and why the third question needs an index on the person column. DynamoDB's single-table design is the far end of this idea: several kinds of record in one table, with related items sharing a partition key so that one query returns them together, an item collection. AWS lists its costs too: the learning curve "can be steep", and data requirements "must be consistent across all entity types". Rollups for dashboards are the same move. Nightwatch's uptime tile can read one row per check per day instead of every result, as long as that rollup is an owned copy with a refresh rule and a check.

diagram.aria: The fix. Sabine's save is one transaction, 4 round trips, 160 ms and 38 rows: first the person row in the person table, the only truth, then her 37 rows in the tree table, which is derived from it. Both commit together or neither does. A nightly check at 03:00 reads the person table, compares all 41,236 tree rows with it, repairs any that differ and alerts. The person page shows 1852 to 1891; her 37 trees agree, and a 400-person tree page still takes 60 ms.

explain.caption: The fix. Save is one transaction: Lavinia's person row first, then her 37 tree rows, and both commit together or not at all. The tree table is derived from the person table and nobody edits it directly. Every night at 03:00 a check compares all 41,236 tree rows with the person table, repairs any that differ and raises an alert. Tree pages still read their own rows: 60 ms for 400 people.

fix.title: The fix: one truth, a refresh in the same transaction, and a nightly check
fix.text: Keep the person table as the only truth, and treat the tree table as a derived copy of it that nobody edits directly. Add an index on the tree table's person column. Change Save into one transaction: update the person row and every tree row for that person, then COMMIT, so the person page and all 37 trees change together: 160 ms and 38 rows for Lavinia. For people in hundreds of trees, write the change to a change queue in the same transaction instead, and let a worker update the trees within a stated delay. Add a nightly check at 03:00 that compares every tree row with the person table, repairs any difference and alerts. Run it once tonight. It will find Lavinia's 37 rows, put her back in the churchyard, and take her off the bench.

limits: A same-transaction refresh grows with the copies. Lavinia's save touches 38 rows; a founder who appears in every tree would touch hundreds, and the save holds a row lock on each until COMMIT. Past some size, a change queue with a stated delay is usually the better trade.

The refresh only covers writes that go through Save. A script, an import or a hand-typed SQL statement that writes the person table directly skips it. A database trigger, or change data capture feeding the queue, puts the refresh where every write passes; the nightly check catches the rest, a day late.

Designing for today's queries makes tomorrow's harder. A table shaped for tree pages answers tree pages fast and other questions badly, and DynamoDB's single-table design takes that furthest: a new access pattern can mean reshaping data, not just adding an index.

explain.seniorTake: Normalize first, then denormalize on purpose, for a read you can name. A copy is safe when it has one owner of the truth, is derived from it and never edited on its own, has a written refresh rule with a stated delay, and has a check that proves it agrees. Pick the rule from the numbers: how often the copy is read, how often the truth changes, how many copies one change touches, and how long a wrong copy may be shown. Same transaction when it must never disagree and the copies are few; a change queue when the copies are many and a short delay is fine; a scheduled rebuild when a day is fine. Start from the queries, not the entities, and write the refresh rule beside every copy you make, because the next person to change the truth will not know the copy exists.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: a materialized view is an owned copy
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's documentation (version 18) says materialized views "use the rule system like views do, but persist the results in a table-like form." Unlike a table created from a query, a materialized view "cannot subsequently be directly updated", and its query is stored, so that fresh data can be generated for it with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. The page is plain about the trade: access to the stored data "is often much faster than accessing the underlying tables directly or through a view", but "the data is not always current; yet sometimes current data is not needed." That is the tree table with an owner and a refresh command.

realWorld.title: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW replaces everything
realWorld.text: The REFRESH page says the command "completely replaces the contents of a materialized view" and "The old contents are discarded." Without CONCURRENTLY, a refresh which affects a lot of rows "could block other connections which are trying to read from the materialized view." With CONCURRENTLY, concurrent selects are not locked out, but it is only allowed if there is "at least one UNIQUE index on the materialized view which uses only column names and includes all rows", and "only one REFRESH at a time may run against any one materialized view." A full refresh is the nightly rebuild: right when it finishes, out of date in between. To change only the rows one correction touches, you update a table of your own, as Kesia does.

realWorld.title: AWS: know the questions before the schema
realWorld.text: AWS's NoSQL design guide for DynamoDB contrasts the two habits. "In RDBMS, you design for flexibility without worrying about implementation details or performance. Query optimization generally doesn't affect schema design, but normalization is important." In DynamoDB, "you design your schema specifically to make the most common and important queries as fast and as inexpensive as possible." Its rule: "you shouldn't start designing your schema for DynamoDB until you know the questions it will need to answer." It asks you to know three properties of the access patterns first: data size, data shape and data velocity. On shape: "Instead of reshaping data when a query is processed (as an RDBMS system does), a NoSQL database organizes data so that its shape in the database corresponds with what will be queried."

realWorld.title: AWS: single-table design and its costs
realWorld.text: AWS's data modeling foundations page says "Single table design is a pattern that allows you to store multiple types (entities) of data in a single DynamoDB table." It works because DynamoDB stores items with the same partition key, an item collection, on the same partitions. The advantages it lists include answering queries across entity types in one call, because items read together sit on the same partitions; its example is that one query for two small items costs half the read units of two separate queries. The disadvantages: "Learning curve can be steep due to paradoxical design compared to relational databases", and "Data requirements must be consistent across all entity types": backups, for one, are all or nothing. And: "If your application's access patterns do not have the need to query multiple entities or tables together, then multiple table design is a good and sufficient approach."

realWorld.title: Codd, 1970: redundancy and consistency
realWorld.text: E. F. Codd, of IBM's research laboratory in San Jose, published "A relational model of data for large shared data banks" in Communications of the ACM, volume 13, issue 6, June 1970, pages 377 to 387. The abstract opens: "Future users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organized in the machine". It introduces relations and "a normal form for data base relations", and it applies them to "the problems of redundancy and consistency in the user's model." Lavinia's two death dates are that problem.

realWorld.title: Kent, 1983: five normal forms in plain words
realWorld.text: William Kent's "A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory" appeared in Communications of the ACM 26(2), February 1983. "The normalization rules are designed to prevent update anomalies and data inconsistencies." He is as clear about the cost: the guidelines "tend to penalize retrieval, since data which may have been retrievable from one record in an unnormalized design" may have to come from several, and "there is no obligation to fully normalize all records when actual performance requirements are taken into account." His summary of second and third normal form, typo included as printed: "a non-key field must provide a fact about the key, us the whole key, and nothing but the key".

asked: Design the schema for this feature, starting from its queries.
How do you keep a denormalized copy correct?
interview.answer: Start with the queries: list each one with how often it runs, how fast it must be, and how fresh its answer must be, and list the writes the same way. Then model the facts normalized: each fact once, in the table it's about, related by keys, so there is one owner of the truth and no update anomalies. Denormalize only for a named read that the normalized form can't serve fast enough, such as a 400-person tree page that takes 1,640 ms built by joins and 60 ms from its own rows. Every copy then needs three things: it is derived from the truth and never edited on its own; it has a refresh rule with a stated delay, either in the same transaction as the write (never wrong, bigger writes), from a change queue or change data capture (small writes, seconds behind), or a scheduled rebuild or materialized view refresh (simple, up to a day behind); and a check that compares copy with truth and alerts. Put the refresh where every write passes, or scripts and imports will skip it. In DynamoDB the same thinking goes further: you design the keys from the access patterns, often in one table with item collections, and accept that a new query may mean reshaping data. Dashboards are the common case: rollups are owned copies with a refresh rule.

terms.def: A club of people researching their family history. Thornleigh's members share a database of people and build family trees from it.
A church's book of baptisms, marriages and burials. Wynfrith types old ones into the society's database; one showed Lavinia's burial in 1891.
An official count of everyone living somewhere, taken every few years. 1900's is the year of the society's farmhouse photograph.
Thornleigh's table of people: one row each, with name, birth, death and parents. It is the society's source of truth. Lavinia's row is P-20417.
The page that shows one person, read from the person table. Sabine corrected Lavinia's death date there.
Alcuin's 2014 table: one row per person per tree they appear in, with a copy of their name, dates and parents. 412 trees, 41,236 rows.
The page that draws one family tree from its rows in the tree table, and names everyone alive in each of the society's photographs.
When a fact is stored in several places and a change reaches only some of them, so the copies go out of step and the data contradicts itself.
The same fact stored more than once. It can make reads faster, and it makes every change a change to every copy.
To store each fact once, in the table it is about, and refer to it by its key everywhere else. The result is normalized data.
Designing tables so that each fact is stored once, in one place, related by keys. Normal forms are its rules.
A rule a table design can meet, numbered first, second, third and beyond. Each one removes a kind of repeated fact.
Every field holds a single value: no lists or repeating groups inside a row, so all rows of a table have the same fields.
No field is a fact about only part of a key made of several columns. A person's name in a table keyed by tree and person breaks it.
No field is a fact about another non-key field, such as a parent's name stored beside the parent's id.
A column that is not part of the table's key, such as a person's death date in the tree table.
Several values of the same kind packed into one row, such as child1, child2, child3. First normal form moves them to rows of their own.
A key made of more than one column. The tree table's rows are identified by tree and person together.
Codd's 1970 idea of storing data as tables of rows (relations) related by keys, queried without knowing how the data is laid out on disk.
Relational database management system: a database built on the relational model, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL.
Storing a copy of facts that live elsewhere, on purpose, to make a read faster. It trades cheaper reads for more work on every change.
Data made from the source of truth and never edited on its own, so it can always be rebuilt from the source.
The written rule for when and how a copy is brought back in line with its source: in the same transaction, from a queue, or on a schedule.
A queue of changes written in the same transaction as the change itself; a worker reads it and updates the copies afterwards.
A job that rebuilds a whole copy from its source every night. Thornleigh's would read at 02:00 and swap in at 02:40.
A job that compares every copy with the source of truth, here at 03:00, repairs any that differ and raises an alert.
A stored query result kept like a table, so reading it is fast. In PostgreSQL it changes only when refreshed.
The PostgreSQL command that reruns a materialized view's query and replaces its whole contents.
A REFRESH option that lets reads continue during the refresh. It needs a unique index on the materialized view.
An index that also refuses two rows with the same value in its columns.
Code the database runs by itself when a row is inserted, updated or deleted, inside the same transaction as that change.
Reading a database's own record of committed changes and passing each change on, such as to a queue, whatever wrote it.
One question an application asks of its data, with how often and how fast, such as show one tree or list a person's trees.
Databases that don't use the relational model's tables and joins, such as DynamoDB. They answer a few planned questions very fast.
In DynamoDB, keeping several kinds of record in one table, with keys chosen so that items read together sit together.
In DynamoDB, one table per kind of record, closer to a relational design. Queries across tables need separate reads.
One kind of thing an application stores, such as a person or a tree. AWS's DynamoDB pages call record types entities.
In DynamoDB, all items that share a partition key. They are stored together, so one query can return them all.
A table of totals made from detailed rows, such as one uptime row per check per day, so a dashboard reads a few rows, not millions.
A person row's pointer to a parent's row by key. Building a tree from the person table follows them a generation at a time.
Round trips to the database for one correction times 40 ms each. It doesn't count a volunteer's minutes.
How many rows one correction writes: the person row, any tree rows, and a queue row if there is one.
The monthly journal of the Association for Computing Machinery, where Codd's 1970 paper and Kent's 1983 guide appeared.

atWork: Picture a common incident: a sales dashboard's revenue tile was a copy, a table of daily totals a job filled every night, and after a run of refunds made with a script, the tile and the finance ledger disagreed for weeks before anyone compared them. Look for the same in your systems. List every copy of data that lives somewhere else too: a denormalized column, a summary or rollup table, a materialized view, a cache, a spreadsheet someone exports. For each, write down four things: which table owns the truth, what derives the copy, its refresh rule and delay, and what checks that copy and truth agree. Then find the writes that go around the refresh: scripts, imports, admin SQL. Any copy without all four is Alcuin's tree table. This rehearses Nightwatch's N2 Build Night, where uptime dashboards read rollups instead of millions of check results: build the rollup as an owned copy, refreshed from the raw results by a rule you write down, with a check that recomputes a day from raw results and compares, and record that decision in docs/decisions.md. If your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes the processing integrity category, its criteria (PI1.3 in the AICPA's 2017 Trust Services Criteria) expect data to be processed completely, accurately and timely as authorized; owned copies with a refresh rule and a reconciliation that alerts are the kind of control an auditor will ask you to show, so build them in from the first schema rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: A support tool's ticket list shows each customer's plan, Free or Pro, beside every ticket. To keep the list fast, the plan was written onto each ticket row when the ticket was opened. A customer upgraded to Pro on Monday; on Wednesday her 40 open tickets still say Free and sit in the slow lane. What went wrong, and how would you fix it without making the list slow?

keyIdeas.idea: The plan is stored in many places and the upgrade changed only the customer's row: an update anomaly, the copies are out of step
The customer table is the one owner of the plan, and the ticket column is a copy derived from it
Give the copy a refresh rule (same transaction, a change queue, a trigger) and a check that finds drift

recall.model: The plan lives in 41 places: the customer's row and a copy on each of her 40 open tickets. The upgrade changed only the customer's row, so the copies are out of step: an update anomaly. Keep the copy, because it's what makes the list fast, but make the customer table the one owner of the plan and treat the ticket column as derived from it. Then give it a refresh rule: update her open tickets in the same transaction as the upgrade, with an index on the tickets' customer id so that's one quick statement, or put the change on a change queue that a worker applies within seconds. Add a nightly check that compares the copies with the customer table and alerts on any difference, and repair today's 40 now.

recall.prompt: Thornleigh's nightly rebuild reads the person table at 02:00 and swaps the new tree table in at 02:40. A member corrects a death date at 02:10 on Monday. When do her trees first show it?
recall.why: Monday's rebuild read the person table at 02:00, before her save, so Monday's 02:40 swap installs copies with the old date. Tuesday's 02:00 reading has it, and the trees show it at 02:40 on Tuesday, 1 d 0 h 30 min after the save. A scheduled rebuild's window runs up to a day plus the rebuild's own length.

recall.prompt: Alcuin's tree table has one row per tree and person, keyed by both columns together, and each row stores the person's name and dates. Which normal form does that break, by William Kent's definitions?
options: None, because the key covers every column
recall.why: Kent: "Second normal form is violated when a non-key field is a fact about a subset of a key." The name and dates are facts about the person alone, half of the tree-and-person key, so they repeat in every tree the person is in. That repetition is what let Lavinia's 37 tree rows disagree with her person row.

recall.prompt: According to AWS's NoSQL design guide, when should you start designing a DynamoDB schema?
options: Once the data is in third normal form
Once you've chosen a partition key with many values
Once you've measured the read and write units you need
Once you know the questions it will need to answer
recall.why: The guide says "you shouldn't start designing your schema for DynamoDB until you know the questions it will need to answer." In a relational database you can normalize first and add queries later; in DynamoDB the keys are shaped by the access patterns, so the list of queries comes first. Partition keys and capacity follow from it.

recall.prompt: Nightwatch's dashboard shows each check's uptime for the last 30 days. Every tile reads up to 43,200 results per check, and the page has slowed to 9 seconds. A teammate proposes a daily_uptime table: one row per check per day, with counts of passes and failures. What must be true for this copy to be safe, and how do you keep it right?

keyIdeas.idea: The raw results stay the source of truth; the rollup is derived from them and can be rebuilt from them
A refresh rule with a stated delay: add each result to its day's row in the same transaction or from a queue, including late results
A check compares the rollup with the raw results and alerts on drift

recall.model: The raw check results stay the source of truth, and daily_uptime is derived from them: one owner, and the rollup can be rebuilt from the raw results at any time. Give it a refresh rule: add each result to its day's row in the same transaction that writes the result, or from a queue within a minute, and say how stale the dashboard may be. Late results land on earlier days, so the rule must update those rows too. Then a nightly check recomputes yesterday's rows from the raw results, compares them with the rollup, and alerts on any drift.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Since Kesia's change, every Save updates the person row and her tree rows in one transaction, and the 03:00 check has found nothing, night after night. In March we merged with the Wickenden society. Their volunteers had kept 2,000 corrections in a spreadsheet, and one of them loaded them at 19:00 with an SQL script from her laptop: one UPDATE person statement per line. At 03:00 the check reported 1,214 tree rows that differed from the person table, and repaired them. All evening, members had seen the old dates in their trees, and two wrote in to ask why their family had gone back to the way it was.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the check find 1,214 rows, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The script wrote the person table directly, not through Save, so the refresh, which lived in the app, never ran
Put the refresh where every write passes: a database trigger, change data capture, or one function all writes must use
Run the check (or a rebuild) straight after any bulk load, with an alert, rather than waiting for 03:00

coldCase.model: The SQL script wrote the person table directly and never went through the save path, so the code that refreshes tree rows in the same transaction never ran: the refresh lived only in the app code, and every write that bypasses Save bypasses it too. The check did its job, eight hours late. Move the refresh to where every write passes: a database trigger on the person table that updates the tree rows in the same transaction, or change data capture feeding the change queue, or a rule that all writes go through one function. And make every bulk load run the check, or rebuild the tree table, as soon as it finishes, with an alert, so nobody waits for 03:00.
